title: Verifier‑Assisted versus One‑Shot LLM Intent→Configuration: A Paired NetOpsTraceBench Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed NetOpsTraceBench, a paired comparison of a one‑shot LLM intent→configuration pipeline and a verifier‑assisted generate–validate–repair pipeline on 1,200 intent→config episodes. Using gpt-5-mini, a deterministic NetOps validator, and Mininet‑style emulation, we applied a preregistered binary episode success rule (validator accepts final config AND emulator shows no availability degradation above tolerance AND no automatic rollback). Of 1,200 planned paired tasks we completed 1,199 pairs. Baseline success = 1,196/1,199 (0.9974979149); guarded success = 1,199/1,199 (1.0000000000). The paired‑success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0025020851 (95% bootstrap percentile CI [0.0000, 0.0058381985], bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10,000); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25. The preregistered power target sought a 5 percentage‑point minimum detectable effect; given the observed near‑ceiling baseline, the study lacked power to detect much smaller absolute gains. Representative validator traces and provider audit logs show repair was invoked only three times. Under these controlled emulation and task‑corpus conditions we find no statistically significant advantage for the verifier‑assisted pipeline; we report artifacts, an explicit preregistration‑to‑analysis disclosure (including an unexecuted preregistered subgroup H3), and execution accounting to support reproducible interpretation.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent expressed in natural language into executable device configurations for network operations (NetOps). Systems and survey literature emphasize that operational reliability depends critically on orchestration, deterministic validators, and assurance infrastructure rather than on an LLM alone [1,2]. Generate–validate–repair (verifier‑assisted) architectures are a canonical mitigation strategy: an LLM proposes candidate outputs, an automated verifier checks constraints and safety, and an automated repair loop iterates until the candidate satisfies verifier rules [3–5]. Despite conceptual support, publicly archived, preregistered, paired evidence measuring whether verifier assistance yields an operationally meaningful improvement (rollback‑aware binary success) relative to one‑shot generation is sparse.

We address this gap with NetOpsTraceBench: a preregistered, paired, emulator‑grounded study comparing (A) baseline one‑shot NL→config generation and (B) a guarded generate–validate–repair pipeline using the same shared initial candidate. The study asked: Can a reproducible, workflow‑centered benchmark of paired intent→config episodes produce an objective paired binary success metric that reliably distinguishes verifier‑assisted pipelines from one‑shot generation across two simulated topologies? Our contributions are (1) a preregistered experimental design and full execution artifacts (study ID rX4f7-1); (2) a paired analysis on 1,199 completed pairs using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator; and (3) transparent reporting of an analytic deviation (Wilcoxon → exact McNemar for binary outcomes), execution accounting that explains why the guarded pipeline rarely required repair, and an explicit disclosure that the preregistered topology‑cluster confirmatory subgroup (H3) was not executed as a confirmatory analysis and remains unexecuted in the archived confirmatory artifacts.
sections.related_work:
Recent surveys and system papers frame LLMs as components inside broader AIOps/NetOps workflows and repeatedly emphasize that correctness and trustworthiness are properties of the entire orchestration stack (model + verifier + provenance + sandboxed execution), not of the base LLM alone [1,2]. Multiple community reviews urge workflow‑centered evaluation—trace quality, validator interactions, and rollback‑aware metrics—rather than isolated one‑shot QA tests; these reviews motivate reproducible, audit‑ready benchmarks that combine generation, deterministic validation, and emulation [1,2,4].

Concrete verifier‑assisted approaches appear across adjacent domains and NetOps prototypes. Work on NL→formal translations and CTL/specification generation demonstrates generator+verifier loops where formal checks drive iterative repairs; similarly, topology‑compilation systems translate high‑level security intent into executable topologies with compliance checks and constraint enforcement [5,6]. Prototype efforts in configuration (text→config generators and misconfiguration detectors) and domain‑specific “LLM firewalls” illustrate practical patterns: an LLM proposes a candidate, an automated validator enforces syntactic and semantic constraints, and an orchestrator optionally triggers constrained repair or rejects the proposal [7–10].

Empirical and conceptual studies document LLM failure modes that motivate guarded architectures: hallucination, unit/semantic errors, overconfidence/miscalibration, provenance loss, and prompt‑injection susceptibility are recurrent risks when LLMs propose executable artifacts [11–14]. Prior work demonstrates verifier‑guided repair reduces some syntactic and semantic errors in constrained settings but highlights sensitivity to verifier rule design and dataset representativeness. These findings motivated our preregistered paired design and deterministic logging to make repair invocation and discordances observable rather than inferred.
sections.methodology:
Overview and preregistration: The study was preregistered as NetOpsTraceBench (study_id = rX4f7-1) and the preregistration manifest (SHA‑256 = 77abe8b493bde44484e0b3d02cfd7f9ec1621ff7e7847889082ae177a7ed5712) froze the experimental plan before any model calls. Confirmatory hypotheses included H1 (primary paired success difference), H2 (failure‑mode cataloging), and H3 (paired breakdown across two topology clusters: edge vs core). The preregistration, inclusion/exclusion rules, seeds, and analysis executor are archived.

Task corpus and paired design: The benchmark scope defined 1,200 distinct operator‑intent tasks split into two simulated topology clusters (edge=600, core=600). Each task was generated deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 using frozen per‑task seeds and carries structured payloads (initial_state, expected_final_state, required_sequence, workflow_policies, and declared difficulty). Per preregistration each task produced two paired episodes that share a single initial candidate (generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate"). We intentionally used shared_initial_candidate semantics so the paired contrast isolates verifier + repair effects while holding generation variability constant across conditions.

Pipeline semantics: Adapter orchestration used hosted_netops_gvr_v1. The requested model was gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json). For each pair the LLM produced one shared_initial_candidate (initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1). Baseline (one‑shot) condition recorded that candidate and proceeded to deterministic parsing/emulation without invoking repair. Guarded (verifier‑assisted) condition validated the same candidate with deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and invoked at most one automated repair call if the validator rejected the candidate (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). Validator scoring used the rule "full_intent_constraint_validation"; validator traces include validation_before/validation_after, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation codes, and repair_applied flags. All provider traces, repair prompts, and validator artifacts are archived.

Contamination, exclusions, and analysis plan: Conservative contamination detection was preregistered (substring/token overlap threshold T_contam = 0.85 and optional embedding check). Automatic exclusion rules and the missingness plan are archived. The primary estimand is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistration specified a paired confirmatory test and bootstrap CI; because outcomes are binary the archived confirmatory analysis executed an exact McNemar two‑sided test and computed a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000). Key analysis artifacts supporting the primary result are archived at analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/results.json, and analysis/analysis_log.jsonl; the execution manifest is execution/execution_manifest.json. NOTE (preregistered subgroup H3): the preregistered topology‑cluster confirmatory breakdown (H3) was not executed as a confirmatory subgroup test and no per‑cluster confirmatory artifacts are present in the archived analysis outputs. We therefore treat H3 as unexecuted for confirmatory inference (see Results and Disclosure).
sections.results:
Execution and accounting: The run completed 2,398 of 2,400 planned episodes and produced 1,199 complete paired observations (complete_pair_count = 1,199; failed_episode_count = 2). Provider audit shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 1,203 (completed = 1,202; failed = 1) and stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 1,200 and repair = 3, indicating repair was invoked only three times.

Primary confirmatory outcomes: The 2×2 paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 1,196 (both succeeded), n10 = 3 (guarded succeeded; baseline failed), n01 = 0 (baseline succeeded; guarded failed), n00 = 0 (both failed). From these counts: baseline_success_count = 1,196 (baseline_success_rate = 1,196/1,199 = 0.9974979149291076) and guarded_success_count = 1,199 (guarded_success_rate = 1,199/1,199 = 1.0). Paired‑success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002502085070892446.

Confirmatory inference: Exact McNemar two‑sided test (on discordant pairs n10 = 3, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.25. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI computed with bootstrap_seed = 1729 and 10,000 resamples is [0.0000, 0.005838198498748957]. The CI lower bound at zero and the small discordant count reflect near‑ceiling baseline performance and limited resolution for small absolute effects.

Missingness and exclusions: analysis/missingness_summary.csv reports complete_pairs = 1,199; failed_baseline_episodes = 1; failed_guarded_episodes = 1; both_missing_pairs = 1. analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty (no automatic contamination exclusions). The single dropped pair accounts for the difference between planned (1,200) and completed (1,199) pairs.

Repair diagnostics and representative artifacts: repair = 3 matches repair provider traces present for exactly three episodes in execution/provider_calls. Representative scoring artifacts (execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json) show identical shared_initial_candidate content and validator traces with validation_after.valid = true and repair_applied = false for many tasks. Representative task manifests show declared difficulty labels ("medium", "hard", "very_hard"); despite heterogeneous declared difficulty the initial candidates often passed the deterministic validator under the chosen validator rules. All numbers above match archived artifacts: analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/results.json, and execution/execution_manifest.json.

Preregistered subgroup H3 (topology clusters): The preregistration specified confirmatory subgroup checks across edge vs core clusters (H3). The archived confirmatory analysis artifacts do not include per‑cluster contingency tables or per‑cluster inference outputs; no per‑cluster confirmatory results are present in analysis/*. The absence of per‑cluster artifacts indicates H3 was not executed as a confirmatory test. This is a preregistration‑to‑analysis mismatch we explicitly disclose: H3 remains unexecuted for confirmatory inference and should be treated as an untested preregistered subgroup in this report. Per‑cluster exploratory analyses can be derived from raw task manifests and per‑episode scoring artifacts in the archive but were not included in the archived confirmatory outputs.
sections.discussion:
Statistical and operational interpretation: The exact McNemar test and bootstrap CI indicate no statistically significant advantage for the guarded pipeline under this corpus and validator configuration (p = 0.25; 95% CI includes zero). Two artifact‑grounded explanations are supported. First, near‑ceiling baseline performance (≈99.75%) constrained headroom; the preregistered MDE was 5 percentage points so the run was not powered to detect an observed ≈0.25 percentage‑point effect. The archived discordant counts (n10 = 3, n01 = 0) and bootstrap CI quantify this limitation. Second, corpus and validator design materially affected repair invocation. Deterministic task generation (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) produced clear required sequences and the deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) accepted most initial candidates; stage_counts and validator traces jointly support that design choice reduced measured repair frequency.

Implications for benchmarking and future work: When initial generation already meets deterministic verifier criteria for common, well‑specified tasks, generate–validate–repair will be infrequently exercised and measured gains on a binary success metric will be small. To evaluate verifier value robustly, future benchmarks should (a) include adversarial and ambiguous intent prompts to increase baseline error rates, (b) vary verifier strictness and parsing rules, and (c) test multiple model families. Our archived artifacts (responses, provider traces, validator traces, task manifests, execution/execution_manifest.json, analysis/*) provide reproducible inputs for such sensitivity studies without new generation calls if alternate analyses are restricted to existing artifacts.

Threats to validity: Internal validity is strong for deterministic components (frozen seeds, deterministic task generation, and automated exclusion rules). Construct validity depends on whether the binary success rule (validator acceptance + emulator availability tolerance + no rollback) maps to operationally meaningful correctness across production environments. External validity is limited by single model family (gpt-5-mini), synthetic/consented tasks, and Mininet‑style emulation. Conclusion validity: low discordant counts imply limited power to detect small absolute differences; interpret the null result in light of the preregistered MDE.

Methodological note on shared_initial_candidate: We selected a shared_initial_candidate paired design to isolate the verifier/repair effect from generation variability. This design intentionally reduces variance due to stochastic generation and makes the paired comparison conservative for measuring repair value because both conditions start from the identical candidate; consequently, repair invocation can be low when the single candidate is already valid under the deterministic verifier. This choice is documented in the preregistration and is reflected in stage_counts (shared_initial_generation = 1,200; repair = 3).
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed NetOpsTraceBench, a paired, emulator‑grounded study comparing one‑shot and verifier‑assisted NL→configuration pipelines on 1,199 completed pairs. Under our synthetic task corpus, deterministic validator settings, and requested model gpt-5-mini, baseline one‑shot generation achieved near‑ceiling success (≈99.75%). The guarded pipeline increased absolute success by ≈0.25 percentage points (paired difference = 0.0025020851) with exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25 and a 95% bootstrap CI that includes zero. Archived execution manifests, provider audits (model_calls_used = 1,203; repairs invoked = 3), representative validator traces, and analysis artifacts support the interpretation that the observed null result reflects limited headroom given task and verifier choices rather than definitive evidence that verifiers are never useful. The preregistered topology subgroup (H3) was not executed as a confirmatory analysis and remains unexecuted in the archived confirmatory artifacts; future work should perform per‑cluster and adversarial sensitivity studies using the archived artifact base. All run artifacts, analysis code, seeds, and logs are archived to enable exact reproduction and follow‑up sensitivity analyses (see Disclosure Statement).

disclosure_statement:
Mandatory disclosure (preregistered run rX4f7-1). LLM(s) and provider: requested model = gpt-5-mini via provider recorded as openai_responses; model configuration archived at execution/model_configuration.json (requested_model=gpt-5-mini, max_output_tokens=1500). Orchestration/adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1 executed the paired benchmark. Deterministic tooling: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performed canonical parsing, intent‑constraint validation, and emulator preflight checks; deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 produced synthetic tasks. Exact initial master prompt: archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (immutable reference SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Topic constraint and autonomy boundary: the human Research Director selected the topic family and approved the master prompt pre‑lock; after the autonomy lock the AI autonomously formulated the research question, conducted literature review, generated the preregistration, executed the experiment, performed analysis, and wrote and revised the manuscript.

Preregistration: NetOpsTraceBench (ID rX4f7-1) preregistration manifest SHA‑256 = 77abe8b493bde44484e0b3d02cfd7f9ec1621ff7e7847889082ae177a7ed5712; preregistered design (confirmatory hypotheses, inclusion/exclusion, seeds, stopping rules, analysis plan) was frozen before execution. Execution summary: started 2026-08-30T01:21:55.415955+00:00, completed 2026-08-30T03:15:12.141890+00:00; planned episodes 2,400; completed episodes 2,398; completed pairs 1,199; model_calls_used = 1,203; repair-stage calls observed = 3. Analysis artifacts and deviation record: the preregistration specified a Wilcoxon signed‑rank paired procedure; the archived executed confirmatory analysis used an exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired binary outcomes plus a paired bootstrap percentile CI. This post‑preregistration analytic choice is documented in analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/results.json, analysis/analysis_log.jsonl, and analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg produced by the run that completed at 2026-08-30T03:15:12.141890+00:00.

Preregistered subgroup H3 (topology cluster breakdown): The preregistration included H3 (confirmatory paired breakdown across edge vs core clusters). The archived confirmatory analysis artifacts do not contain per‑cluster contingency tables or per‑cluster inferential outputs; therefore H3 was not executed as a confirmatory subgroup analysis. This absence is reflected by the lack of per‑cluster analysis files in the archived analysis outputs (analysis/ directory) and is explicitly disclosed here.

Key archived artifacts for primary confirmatory results (machine‑readable pointers): analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/results.json, analysis/analysis_log.jsonl, execution/execution_manifest.json, execution/raw_results.jsonl, and execution/task_manifest.jsonl. The full artifact hash manifest and additional artifacts are archived at execution/execution_manifest.json. Artifacts demonstrate provider_call_audit counts (hosted_model_call_event_count = 1,203), stage_counts (shared_initial_generation = 1,200; repair = 3), and per‑episode validator traces used to compute binary success.

Reproducibility and human involvement: All seeds, task generation code, validator rules, repair prompts, provider traces, and analysis code are published in the run artifacts (artifact_count = 8,408; full hash manifest path recorded in execution/execution_manifest.json). Pre‑lock collaboration and infrastructure development occurred; no human manual editing, selective revision, or ad hoc text insertion occurred on the manuscript content after the autonomy lock—the AI performed internal autonomous revision cycles only. Technical restarts and deviations: execution manifest records two failed episodes and the analytic deviation described above; all deviations are logged in execution/execution_log.jsonl. The disclosure above is complete relative to the archived artifacts supplied with this run.
limitations: Single model family tested (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across other LLMs or fine‑tuned variants.
Task corpus skew: synthetic/consented tasks yielded near‑ceiling baseline success (≈99.75%), limiting headroom and statistical power to detect practical improvements by guarded pipelines.

Emulator fidelity: Mininet‑style emulation and deterministic validators approximate production behavior but may not capture all deployment failure modes (routing convergence, vendor idiosyncrasies, transient telemetry).

Verifier configuration dependence: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 acceptance thresholds and parsing rules materially affect outcomes; different verifier strictness could change repair invocation rates and measured gains.

Analytic deviation documented: the preregistration specified a Wilcoxon signed‑rank paired procedure; the archived confirmatory analysis used an exact McNemar test because outcomes were binary. This deviation is recorded in the archived analysis artifacts and in the Disclosure Statement above.

Preregistered subgroup H3 (topology cluster breakdown) was not executed as a confirmatory analysis and remains untested in the archived confirmatory outputs; per‑cluster exploration was not included in the archived confirmatory artifacts.
